newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers, U.S. officials spar over Azeri ties.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers, U.S. officials spar over Azeri ties.

text.p: Clinton administration officials on Thursday applauded Azerbaijan's open investment climate, while Armenian supporters in Congress complained about U.S. overtures to Azerbaijan.

Eager to ensure that U.S. companies tap into a potential $4 trillion in oil revenues in the former Soviet republic and build up a new oil supply source outside the Middle East, the administration is pushing business ties with Azerbaijan.
At the same time, the United States is working with France and Russia in a bid to resolve the nearly 10-year-old conflict between Armenia and Azerbaijan over the disputed enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh.

In an enthusiastic endorsement of Aliyev, U.S. Commerce Department counsellor Jan Kalicki announced that his department planned to open an office in the Azeri capital, Baku, later this year to help U.S. firms.
"Aliyev is a real friend of American business in Azerbaijan," U.S. ambassador to Azerbaijan Richard Kauzlarich told a gathering of business executives.

While the U.S. officials were touting investments in Azerbaijan, a bipartisan group of lawmakers questioned how the administration could remain impartial in talks between Armenia and Azerbaijan, and slammed Aliyev's human rights record.
President Bill Clinton is set to meet Aliyev on Friday, when the two presidents are expected to discuss the Nagorno-Karabakh dispute.

"Your meeting with President Aliyev will most likely only encourage Azerbaijan to further harden its negotiating stance," 64 House of Representatives members said in a July 30 letter to Clinton released on Thursday. "This encouragement is particularly dangerous given President Aliyev's pattern of unacceptable behaviour"

Aliyev is pressing Washington to repeal a U.S. ban on economic aid to the Azeri government in place since 1992. Clinton opposes the ban, but a strong Armenian-American lobby is fighting to keep it in place.
